question: to the Commission Fabio De Masi (NI) Subject:

The newly established EU AI Office is tasked with monitoring compliance with the Artificial Intelligence Act but has faced criticism for being inadequately equipped1. According to reports, the office currently has no access to advanced models such as Mythos developed by Anthropic, which is reported to potentially outperform human capabilities in detecting software vulnerabilities and could pose risks to critical infrastructure. While the UK AI Security Institute has already presented a technical analysis, the Commission is not among the organisations that were granted access to the model. Furthermore, the office’s safety unit is reported to be understaffed with around 36 employees and to have a relatively low position within the Commission’s hierarchy. 1.
What specific measures is the Commission taking to strengthen the AI Office in terms of staffing, technical expertise and budget, and what measures does it intend to take in the future?
Does the Commission intend to upgrade the office’s institutional position to ensure that it can act independently and respond in the event of an acute cybersecurity crisis?
What political and diplomatic measures does the Commission intend to take to be able to carry out its own technical analysis of Mythos?
https://www.politico.eu/article/anthropic-hacking-technology-exposes-eu-ai-office-struggles/.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The AI Office is a directorate within the Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology (CNECT). The AI Office employs more than 140 staff, including over 40, predominantly technical, staff in the AI Safety Unit, and 35 in the Regulatory and Compliance Unit. There are no plans to change the institutional position of the AI Office within CNECT, which mirrors that of the directorates responsible for enforcing the Digital Services Act1 and the Digital Markets Act2. The Digital Omnibus on AI foresees additional staffing. The next Multiannual Financial Framework, where the Commission has asked for an increase in human resources, will determine staff levels from 2028. On cyber risk, capacity is also located within CNECT’s Directorate for Cybersecurity and the EU Agency for Cybersecurity. Regarding Mythos, Anthropic is a signatory to the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice3 and has committed to assess and mitigate systemic risks, including cybersecurity risks, and submit results to the AI Office. As regulator, the AI Office has held technical meetings with Anthropic to support implementation of the Code. The AI Office has unique access to providers’ internal safety practices and is discussing how to improve them. Where appropriate, it may run its own AI evaluations. The Code also requires companies to work with third-party evaluators – organisations that test AI models for capabilities and risks. Once the AI Office’s enforcement powers apply in August 2026, requests for information, and, if necessary, model access will become mandatory. On 9 June 2026, Anthropic made a safeguarded Mythos-class model, Fable 5, publicly available. After US government’s intervention on 12 June 2026, Anthropic withdrew the model.
